item.research_question: How do powder preparation, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), and microplasma spraying (MPS) affect the phase composition and microstructure of FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 high entropy alloy, and what are the effects of subsequent annealing on these properties?
item.processing_route: Gas atomization (1600 °C melt, 40 bar argon pressure, ~25 μm particles); L-PBF (190 W laser power, 1000 mm/s scanning speed, 100 μm spot size, 40 μm layer thickness, N2 atmosphere); MPS (38 V, 2.3 L/min plasma Ar, 2 L/min carrying Ar, 26 A current); Annealing (600 °C and 900 °C for 1 h in air)
item.test_conditions: XRD (20°–140° 2Θ, 2°/min), SEM/EDS, DTA (20°/min to 900 °C), Vickers microhardness (50 g load, 10 s dwell), Nanoindentation (1500 μN load, 8×8 matrix)
key_findings: Gas atomization produces a supersaturated BCC solid solution with Mo-rich segregations on dendrite peripheries.
L-PBF samples exhibit microstructure and phase composition very similar to the as-atomized powder.
MPS coatings contain a fraction of FCC phase due to Al oxidation and subsequent Al-depletion regions.
Maximum microhardness of 950 HV is achieved in powder and L-PBF samples after annealing at 600 °C.
After annealing at 900 °C, microhardness decreases to approximately 850 HV due to stress relaxation and σ-phase precipitation.
The elastic modulus of the L-PBF sample is 165 GPa, which is 12% lower than that of the cast alloy (186 GPa).
Annealing at 900 °C causes decomposition of the solid solution into B2 and σ-phases.
High-temperature annealing (900 °C) of MPS coatings leads to sample failure due to oxide growth and stress development.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the hardness increase at 600 °C to the growth of elastic stresses between multiple BCC solid solutions caused by increased element segregation. The subsequent decrease at 900 °C is explained by stress relaxation from solid solution decomposition, counterbalanced by the precipitation of hard, homogeneously distributed σ-phase. In MPS coatings, Al oxidation creates Al-depleted regions where the FCC structure becomes thermodynamically stable compared to BCC.
item.limitations: The authors note that the absence of the μ-phase in the cast alloy, despite Thermo-Calc predictions, may be due to extremely low formation rates or insufficient database reliability. Additionally, high-temperature annealing of MPS coatings resulted in partial destruction, limiting the evaluation of their high-temperature stability.
quotes: Maximum hardness (950 HV) is achieved in the powder and L-PBF samples after annealing at 600 °C.
Elastic modulus of the L-PBF sample, determined by nanoindentation, is 165 GPa, that is 12% lower than that of the cast alloy (186 GPa).
The MPS coating has a little fraction of face centered cubic (FCC) phase because of Al oxidation during spraying and formation of regions depleted in Al, in which FCC structure becomes more stable.

Question: How do powder preparation, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), and microplasma spraying (MPS) affect the phase composition and microstructure of FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 high entropy alloy, and what are the effects of subsequent annealing on these properties?. System: FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 (nominal composition FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3). Processing: Gas atomization (1600 °C melt, 40 bar argon pressure, ~25 μm particles); L-PBF (190 W laser power, 1000 mm/s scanning speed, 100 μm spot size, 40 μm layer thickness, N2 atmosphere); MPS (38 V, 2.3 L/min plasma Ar, 2 L/min carrying Ar, 26 A current); Annealing (600 °C and 900 °C for 1 h in air). Test conditions: XRD (20°–140° 2Θ, 2°/min), SEM/EDS, DTA (20°/min to 900 °C), Vickers microhardness (50 g load, 10 s dwell), Nanoindentation (1500 μN load, 8×8 matrix). Findings: Gas atomization produces a supersaturated BCC solid solution with Mo-rich segregations on dendrite peripheries.; L-PBF samples exhibit microstructure and phase composition very similar to the as-atomized powder.; MPS coatings contain a fraction of FCC phase due to Al oxidation and subsequent Al-depletion regions.; Maximum microhardness of 950 HV is achieved in powder and L-PBF samples after annealing at 600 °C.; After annealing at 900 °C, microhardness decreases to approximately 850 HV due to stress relaxation and σ-phase precipitation.; The elastic modulus of the L-PBF sample is 165 GPa, which is 12% lower than that of the cast alloy (186 GPa).; Annealing at 900 °C causes decomposition of the solid solution into B2 and σ-phases.; High-temperature annealing (900 °C) of MPS coatings leads to sample failure due to oxide growth and stress development.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the hardness increase at 600 °C to the growth of elastic stresses between multiple BCC solid solutions caused by increased element segregation. The subsequent decrease at 900 °C is explained by stress relaxation from solid solution decomposition, counterbalanced by the precipitation of hard, homogeneously distributed σ-phase. In MPS coatings, Al oxidation creates Al-depleted regions where the FCC structure becomes thermodynamically stable compared to BCC.. Limitations: The authors note that the absence of the μ-phase in the cast alloy, despite Thermo-Calc predictions, may be due to extremely low formation rates or insufficient database reliability. Additionally, high-temperature annealing of MPS coatings resulted in partial destruction, limiting the evaluation of their high-temperature stability..
